clue.text: POTUS in trouble over wall, finally — that's natural

indicators.note: POTUS, in and the end of wall get into trouble, so their letters are thrown into disorder
finally points to the closing letter of wall

explanation.surface: The US President in a fix over his border wall, presented as somehow the natural state of things.
explanation.walkthrough: POTUS is the President of the United States; 'trouble' scrambles POTUS, IN and the L that ends 'wall', with 'finally' picking that L.
explanation.definitionFit: Something untouched and pristine is still in its original, natural condition.

clue.text: Old music producer very likely showing up

indicators.note: up in a down answer says the letters are read from bottom to top
showing says the letters are on display inside the words very likely

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An old-time record producer is very likely to turn up.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft gave 'showing up' wholly to the reversal; 'showing' is what signals the letters sitting inside 'very likely', and 'up' turns ERYL round in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Greek stringed instrument, so an old producer of music in the literal sense.

clue.text: West coast county supporting government almost every time

indicators.note: in a down answer a supporting piece sits beneath, so G goes on top
almost means the final letter of the synonym is dropped

parts.note: every time means always

explanation.surface: A county on the west coast reliably backs the government at every election.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'supporting government' puts ALWAY (ALWAYS less its last letter) below G.
explanation.definitionFit: A county of the Republic of Ireland lying on its Atlantic western seaboard.

clue.text: Moving date — hurry round on foot

indicators.note: Moving says one letter is shifted to a new spot within the built word
round means the word for hurry goes around on

parts.note: to hurry is to speed

explanation.surface: Someone has moved a date and must hurry round on foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moving' shifts the D (date) inside SPONEED, the letters 'round' makes. 'foot' is the unit of poetic metre, not the body part the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: A metrical foot of two stressed syllables, as in poetry scansion.

clue.text: Mind part of drink before journey

parts.note: to sup is to drink
ere is a poetic word for before
to go is to journey or travel

explanation.surface: Part of one's mind wants a drink before setting off on a trip.
explanation.definitionFit: In Freudian psychology it is the conscience-like component of the psyche.

clue.text: Is extremely upset (tackle's caught in flies)

indicators.note: caught in says the gear is trapped inside the word for flies

parts.note: flies in the sense of rushes, hastens
tackle is kit, as in fishing or sports gear; the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: An angler is beside himself because his tackle is tangled up in the flies.
explanation.definitionFit: A British idiom for being extremely agitated or panicking.

clue.text: On which Jane's voice can be heard

indicators.note: can be heard says a word is spoken and we enter what it sounds like

parts.note: a tenor is a singing voice

explanation.surface: Something on which Jane's singing voice can be heard, like a recording.
explanation.walkthrough: Jane Austen's portrait appears on the Bank of England ten-pound note, colloquially named for its value.
explanation.definitionFit: The British ten-pound banknote bears a portrait of Jane Austen, the novelist.

clue.text: Working-class stripper with Young Conservative — it may be on your phone

parts.note: and means with, plus

parts.words: it may be on your phone
parts.note: an app is a program found on a smartphone

explanation.surface: A working-class stripteaser and a young Tory, perhaps captured on your phone.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'stripper' is a comic-strip figure: the cloth-capped, beer-loving working-class northerner of the Daily Mirror cartoon.
explanation.definitionFit: The long-running British cartoon strip hero is a stereotypical working-class man.

clue.text: We object — A&E's good in practice

parts.note: us is the object form of we

indicators.note: in says the letter for good sits between the two letters

parts.note: A&E, the hospital accident and emergency department, supplies A and E

explanation.surface: We protest: is the hospital's casualty unit actually good in practice?
explanation.definitionFit: Usage means customary practice or habitual way of doing something.

clue.text: Cornish artist reproduced content

indicators.note: content means only the inside of the synonym is kept, its outer letters lost

parts.note: to reproduce is to copy

explanation.surface: A Cornish painter is happy to have his work reproduced.
explanation.walkthrough: John Opie (1761-1807) was a portrait painter born in Cornwall, the county at England's south-western tip.
explanation.definitionFit: John Opie was an eighteenth-century portraitist from Cornwall known as the Cornish Wonder.

clue.text: Young German master's last to kowtow to the bottom form

indicators.note: last to points at the final letter of kowtow

parts.note: beneath, at the bottom, is under
a form or type is a kind

explanation.surface: A young German maestro grovels at the feet of the lowest class.
explanation.definitionFit: A German loanword for a child prodigy, a youthful master of a field.

clue.text: Shame about empty gardens in Berkshire home

indicators.note: about means the word for shame wraps round

parts.note: what a shame is what a pity

indicators.note: empty means gardens loses its insides, leaving its outer letters

explanation.surface: It's a shame the gardens of a Berkshire house have been left bare.
explanation.walkthrough: Berkshire is an English county but also a breed of pig.
explanation.definitionFit: A Berkshire is a pig breed, and the pen where pigs live is their home.

clue.text: Told state's bombarding archipelago

indicators.note: Told means the words are spoken and we enter what they sound like

parts.note: to state is to say, and bombarding is shells, as in shells a target

explanation.surface: We are told a nation is shelling a group of islands.
explanation.definitionFit: An Indian Ocean nation made up of over a hundred islands.

clue.text: Curt mostly follows flat horses

indicators.note: follows says the shortened word comes after the word for flat

parts.note: flat means level, even

indicators.note: mostly drops the final letter of the synonym

parts.note: curt means terse

explanation.surface: A curt verdict mostly follows on the flat racing horses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flat' hints at flat racing, but here it means level.
explanation.definitionFit: Horses that compete in eventing, combining dressage, cross-country and showjumping.

clue.text: Don't move sheep back across river

indicators.note: across means the reversed word spans either side of the river
back means the word for sheep is written in reverse

parts.note: tups are rams, male sheep
the Tay is a Scottish river

explanation.surface: A shepherd is told not to move the sheep back across the river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' makes SPUT, which 'across' wraps around the river; tup is a British word for a ram, and the Tay is Scotland's longest river.
explanation.definitionFit: An imperative phrase meaning remain where you are, a command to stay still.

clue.text: Team built lead going crazy in final

indicators.note: crazy says the pooled letters of team and the shortened word are scrambled
lead going means built loses its leading letter

explanation.surface: A team built up a lead and went wild in the final.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lead going' strips B from 'built', leaving UILT; 'crazy' mixes TEAM with UILT.
explanation.definitionFit: Ultimate is a synonym of last or final, the one at the end.

clue.text: Favour alternative over me? No resistance!

indicators.note: over means the word for alternative is turned round

parts.note: or introduces an alternative

indicators.note: No means the letter for resistance is taken away

parts.note: in crosswords me is the setter
R is the symbol for resistance in physics

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether to favour an alternative over them, and meets no resistance.
explanation.definitionFit: A favour in the old sense is a ribbon or badge worn as a token, as a rosette is.

clue.text: Batters (English) not right for this?

indicators.note: English in place of not right means the letter for right is swapped out
English in place of not right means the letter for right is swapped out

parts.note: batters means thrashes, beats

explanation.surface: English batsmen take part in this, but are they up to it?
explanation.walkthrough: The Ashes is the Test cricket series between England and Australia, so English batters play for it.
explanation.definitionFit: The cricket trophy and series contested by England and Australia, which English batsmen strive for.

clue.text: Birds in tight corsets

indicators.note: tight is slang for drunk, so the letters of corsets reel about

explanation.surface: Birds squeezed into tight corsets.
explanation.definitionFit: Large sea ducks of northern waters, a kind of wildfowl.

clue.text: Woeful epic that's in need of editing

indicators.note: needing to be edited, these letters are rearranged into a new order

parts.note: the 's is the verb is, so the word that is the fodder

explanation.surface: A dreadful epic poem badly needs an editor.
explanation.definitionFit: Pathetic as feeble or wretchedly inadequate, a synonym of woeful.

clue.text: Now pay the price over Cummings's leadership?

indicators.note: over means the word for pay the price covers the initial

parts.note: to atone is to pay the price for a wrong

indicators.note: leadership is the first letter, the head, of Cummings

explanation.surface: Should Dominic Cummings now pay the price for his part in the leadership?
explanation.walkthrough: Dominic Cummings was the chief adviser to Prime Minister Boris Johnson.
explanation.definitionFit: Immediately or without delay, equivalent in sense to now.

clue.text: Stuck in olden days with English definitely at the forefront!

parts.note: the olden days are the past

indicators.note: at the forefront means the first letter of definitely

explanation.surface: Someone definitely stuck in the olden days with English at the front of everything.
explanation.definitionFit: Pasted as stuck on with glue or paste, past participle matching stuck.

clue.text: Roman governor gets a lot of exercise

indicators.note: a lot of means most but not all of the word, its last letter lost

parts.note: Pilates is a system of exercises

explanation.surface: A Roman governor gets plenty of exercise.
explanation.definitionFit: Pontius Pilate, prefect of Judaea who tried Jesus, was a Roman governor.

clue.text: Able to work with molten silver or gold

indicators.note: to work the letters is to knead them like a craftsman into a new form

explanation.surface: A metalworker is able to work with molten silver or gold.
explanation.definitionFit: Precious metals resistant to corrosion are classed chemically under this term; silver and gold are examples.

clue.text: Food is hot but not the whole course

indicators.note: only part of the phrase food is hot is used, so the letters lie within it

explanation.surface: The food is hot but not the entire meal is served yet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Food' wants to be the definition; it is part of the letter string.
explanation.definitionFit: A dish is one course of a meal, such as a main or dessert.

clue.text: It's thrown in hurry

definitions.meaning: a pointed missile thrown at a board in the pub game
to hurry is to dash or move suddenly

explanation.surface: Something is thrown in a hurry.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a small missile for throwing and a verb meaning to dash quickly.

clue.text: Do the acrosses (first two easily)

indicators.note: easily, loosely done, says the letters are rearranged
first two takes the opening pair of letters of acrosses

explanation.surface: Do the across clues, and the first two come easily.
explanation.definitionFit: To do someone is to swindle them, so a synonym of deceive.

clue.text: Flipping costly keeping sailors in drink

indicators.note: keeping means the reversed word holds the sailors inside
Flipping means the word for costly is turned back to front

parts.note: costly means dear
tars is a slang word for sailors

explanation.surface: Flipping costly, keeping the sailors supplied with drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' is a mild British expletive, but here it reverses DEAR to RAED, which takes in TARS.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for very drunk, the state of being in drink.
